key: Place each agent at the one step it stops: anions compete at the symporter, thionamides and iodide excess stop organification, high-dose iodide and lithium slow release, and several drugs and illness block peripheral deiodination.
items: Perchlorate is an anion similar to iodide that competes for the sodium-iodide symporter, so less iodide enters the cell.
Pertechnetate is carried by the symporter like iodide, which is why technetium scans image trapping without organification.
Thiocyanate, from cyanide metabolism in smokers or cassava diets, competitively inhibits iodide transport into the follicular cell.
Methimazole inhibits thyroid peroxidase, so iodide is not attached to tyrosines and iodotyrosines are not coupled.
Carbimazole is a prodrug converted to methimazole, so it blocks thyroid peroxidase exactly as methimazole does.
Excess iodide transiently shuts down organification, a protective reflex that a damaged gland may fail to escape.
Peroxidase gene mutations are the commonest cause of dyshormonogenesis, so iodide is trapped but never organified, causing goiter.
Lithium is concentrated by the gland and inhibits release of T4 and T3 from thyroglobulin, causing goiter and hypothyroidism.
High-dose iodide rapidly inhibits proteolysis of thyroglobulin, so stored hormone stops leaving the gland within hours.
Beyond beta blockade, high-dose propranolol modestly inhibits 5'-deiodinase, lowering conversion of T4 to active T3.
Glucocorticoids inhibit 5'-deiodinase, which is one reason they are given in thyroid storm.
Cytokines, cortisol and fasting inhibit deiodinase, producing the low T3 and high reverse T3 of sick euthyroid syndrome.
